sources.text:
OK so the thing I want to write about is the home lab, which started as a joke really. Over the summer of 2025 I was living in a flat in Sheffield with Josh, who does electronics, and we had a pile of three old mini PCs that his uncle's office was throwing out. I'd been doing a cloud module at uni and wanted somewhere to actually run things instead of just reading about them, so I decided to turn the three boxes into a little cluster that could host the things our course society kept losing: the Discord bot, the website for the weekly meetups and a Minecraft server that honestly got more use than either.

I went with Proxmox on all three nodes because I wanted to be able to break VMs without breaking the box, and then k3s inside VMs for the containers, which in hindsight was probably one layer too many but I learned a lot from it. Everything is built with Ansible playbooks from a git repo so I can rebuild a node from nothing in about twenty minutes, I timed it. Storage is a ZFS mirror on the two nodes that had two disks. Monitoring is Prometheus and Grafana with Alertmanager sending to a Discord webhook, which is a bit silly but it works. Josh set up the Tailscale mesh so we could reach the cluster from uni, and he also lent me the second mini PC's RAM, which I still have not returned.

The decision I keep coming back to is k3s inside Proxmox VMs rather than bare metal. The reason was that I wanted snapshots: I could snapshot a VM, try an upgrade, and roll back when it went wrong, which it did, twice. The cost was performance and a lot of confusion about which layer was eating the memory.

The big problem was in October 2025. The Minecraft server kept freezing for ten or twenty seconds every few minutes. Everyone blamed the game. I spent, I think, two evenings reading Grafana graphs and eventually noticed the freezes lined up with ZFS scrub windows and with the ARC cache growing until the VM started swapping. I had given the VM too much memory relative to the host, so the host was squeezing it. I fixed it by capping the ARC to 4 GB and moving the scrub to 4am on Sundays. The freezes stopped. What I learned is to look at the host before the guest, and that memory accounting across three layers is genuinely hard to reason about.

Anyway, it has been running since then, about 14 months now, with one outage when the flat lost power. The society uses the website and the bot every week. I also wrote a small page that shows the cluster status so people stop asking me in the group chat.

Why Graphcore, I like the layer under the application more than the application itself, and I like that the platform work is about getting the most out of specific hardware rather than generic boxes, which is basically what I was doing with three cast-off PCs except at a slightly different scale.

Also my cat sat on the keyboard during the Ansible rebuild once and it still worked, which I count as a test.

Tell us about a technical system or project you built, configured, automated or troubleshot. This could be a personal project, home lab, university assignment, hackathon or team project, involving hardware, software, networks or cloud services.

In your response, briefly explain:
- What you were trying to achieve.
- The main components or technologies you used.
- One technical decision you made and why.
- One problem you encountered, how you investigated it and what you learned.
- Your individual contribution, if you worked as part of a team.

(Max 300 words)

Over the summer of 2025 I turned three cast-off mini PCs in our Sheffield flat into a small cluster that hosts our course society's Discord bot, website and game server. The society uses the website and the bot every week.

I used Proxmox on all three nodes because I wanted to be able to break VMs without breaking the box, and then k3s inside VMs for the containers. Storage is a ZFS mirror on the two nodes that had two disks. Monitoring is Prometheus and Grafana, with Alertmanager sending to a Discord webhook.

I chose k3s inside Proxmox VMs rather than bare metal. I wanted snapshots so I could snapshot a VM, try an upgrade and roll back when it went wrong, which happened twice.

The Minecraft server kept freezing for ten or twenty seconds every few minutes. I spent two evenings reading Grafana graphs and noticed the freezes lined up with ZFS scrub windows and with ARC cache growing until the VM started swapping. I fixed it by capping the ARC to 4 GB and moving the scrub to 4am on Sundays. I learned to look at the host before the guest, and that memory accounting across three layers is hard.

I can rebuild a node in about twenty minutes because everything is built with Ansible playbooks from a git repo. I set up the Tailscale mesh myself; Josh only lent me the second mini PC's RAM.

Dear Graphcore hiring team,

I am applying for the Graduate Cloud Platform Engineer 2027 role at Graphcore.

I like the layer under the application more than the application itself, and I like that the platform work is about getting the most out of specific hardware rather than generic boxes.

I decided to turn three boxes into a cluster to host the society Discord bot, website and Minecraft server. I used Proxmox on all three nodes and chose k3s inside VMs for containers rather than bare metal. I wanted snapshots so I could try an upgrade and roll back when it went wrong, which happened twice. Everything is built with Ansible playbooks from a git repo, and I can rebuild a node in about twenty minutes. Storage is a ZFS mirror on the two nodes that had two disks. Monitoring is Prometheus and Grafana, with Alertmanager sending to a Discord webhook.

The Minecraft server kept freezing for ten or twenty seconds every few minutes. I spent two evenings reading Grafana graphs and noticed the freezes lined up with ZFS scrub windows and ARC cache growth until the VM started swapping. I fixed it by capping the ARC to 4 GB and moving the scrub to 4am on Sundays. I learned to look at the host before the guest, and that memory accounting across three layers is hard. The society uses the website and the bot every week.

Thank you for considering my application.

Kind regards, Ellie
